summary: Steel light near mid-Lake St. Clair, commissioned 1941 to replace a lightship on the Grosse Pointe passage; Coast Guard property, tower closed to visitors.

lens.type: 375 millimeter lens with electric incandescent lamp

structures.type: steel tower on a steel-piling and concrete foundation

access.note: Coast Guard property; the tower is closed (LighthouseFriends). The U.S. Lighthouse Society lists it as not open to the public.

events.note: Federal lightship LV-10 replaced a privately maintained lightship (LighthouseFriends).
Lightship No. 75 placed on the lake in August 1902 (LighthouseFriends, quoting the Lake Carriers' Association).
Lightship moved farther north and renamed Lake St. Clair (LighthouseFriends).
Lightship rebuilt inside with automatic and remote-controlled apparatus; LighthouseFriends calls it the first radio-controlled lightship in the United States.
Foundation erected as a Public Works Administration project (LighthouseFriends).
Station placed in commission on June 18, 1941 (LighthouseFriends; USLHS 'Year Established: 1941').
Fog signal changed from a diaphragm horn to a bell (LighthouseFriends).
Remote weather station operated on the lighthouse for several years, disestablished May 16, 2011 (LighthouseFriends).

keepers.name: Joseph DesJardins
keepers.note: Spelled DesJardins in the Detroit Times (20 Feb 1909) and Desjardins in LighthouseFriends. The Times gives his post as mate of the Grosse Pointe lightship; LighthouseFriends gives sixteen years' service and a dismissal in 1909 for conduct on Christmas Eve while the ship was moored for the winter. The 'from' year (about 1893) is derived by subtracting the sixteen years from 1909; no dated source gives it.

notes_for_editor: (1) first_lit: the record gives 1878 (Rowlett). No source read confirms a 1878 lighting. LighthouseFriends dates the 1878 scow LV-10 and places the lightship replacement in 1887, so 1878 may be a build date. The story gives 1941 as the lighthouse's first lighting. (2) Status conflict: the USLHS record says 'Active Aid to Navigation?: No'. A Coast Guard Historian's page appeared in search (archived copy not readable in this session) with 'Operational: Y'. Check the current Coast Guard Light List before the page states whether the light is lit; the story reports only what the USLHS record says. (3) Duplicate lightship record: us-mi-lake-st-clair-2 (lightship station, status lost) covers the 1887-1941 lightship years that this story also tells; the editor may want to cross-link or merge. (4) Lightship numbers: LighthouseFriends says No. 75 from 1902. The Commissioner's fiscal-year tables (volume 1915-1922) list a 'Lake St. Clair Light Vessel No. 75' in one table and 'Lake St. Clair Light Vessel, 102' in another; the years of those tables were not resolved, so the story gives no number after 1902. (5) Desjardins: the Times OCR is damaged at the place where it gives his years, so 'sixteen years' comes from LighthouseFriends only. The Times' rescue account is undated ('several years' earlier). (6) The 1941 Lake Carriers' Association description is quoted through LighthouseFriends; the original report was not read. (7) No USLHS roster exists for this station ('ROSTER: none listed'), so keepers are only those named in the sources. (8) LighthouseFriends is an all-rights-reserved site: the story paraphrases it and uses short quotations only. (9) The Coast Guard owns the light; it is closed to visitors per LighthouseFriends. No boat-access claim beyond 'best viewed from the water' is made. (10) Fact-check 2026-10-28: the item is in the Bulletin's January 1937 issue and says only 'the beginning of December', so the ice is most likely December 1936, not December 1937 (the story gives no year and cites the issue). (11) The nautical-mile figure ('six nautical miles') was removed: LighthouseFriends gives 'roughly seven miles' with no unit. (12) The 1894 'expected to do without it' wording was replaced by the report's own conditional ('could be discontinued' once the channel is lighted at each end on cribs).
